If someone is obdurate, they are stubbornly and completely unwilling to change their mind, attitude, or behavior — even when faced with very good reasons, emotional appeals, or moral arguments to do so. Think of their mind as a wall: you can knock on it, reason with it, beg it, cry in front of it — and it simply will not budge.
The heart of the word — and what makes it special

Many words describe stubbornness, but "obdurate" is a cut above. It doesn't just mean someone is stubborn in a casual, ordinary way. It carries a sense of hardness of heart. An obdurate person isn't simply forgetting to change — they are consciously, actively refusing to be moved, and often in situations where most reasonable or compassionate people would be moved. This is why the word has a strong moral weight to it. It implies a kind of coldness or indifference to persuasion, emotion, or conscience.
Two closely related shades of meaning

The word works in two situations, both rooted in the same core idea of being unmovable:

The first is intellectual stubbornness — refusing to change a decision, opinion, or course of action even when others present compelling arguments or beg you to reconsider. For example, a landlord who refuses to lower rent despite knowing his tenants are struggling financially, no matter how much they plead, is being obdurate.

The second shade is moral hardness or lack of remorse — being so hardened that you feel no guilt, regret, or shame for something you have done wrong. For example, a criminal who sits in a courtroom and shows zero remorse, completely untouched by the gravity of their crime, could be described as obdurate. This second shade was historically more common, but today both senses are used.

What unites both shades is the image of someone who has heard everything there is to hear — the arguments, the tears, the moral case — and has remained completely, almost unnaturally, unmoved.

"Obdurate" is a formal word. You will encounter it more in writing — literary fiction, newspapers, legal and political commentary, formal speeches — than in everyday conversation. Using it signals that you are speaking with precision and weight. It is not the kind of word you'd use lightly to describe someone who simply won't share the TV remote.
How it compares to similar words

Understanding a word also means knowing how it differs from its neighbors.

Stubborn is the most everyday word and the most neutral of the group. A stubborn child refusing to eat vegetables is mildly annoying, but we don't necessarily think of them as morally flawed.

Obstinate is a step stronger than stubborn. It suggests persistence in refusing, often unreasonably, and carries a more negative tone.

Obdurate is the strongest and most formal of the three. It implies not just that someone refuses to budge, but that they are doing so with a kind of hardened indifference — often to emotional or moral pressure specifically. An obdurate person isn't just being difficult; they are being unyielding in a way that feels cold or even callous.

Adamant means firmly insisting on something and can sometimes be used in a neutral or even admirable sense ("she was adamant about protecting the children"). Obdurate almost never carries a positive sense.

Intransigent means refusing to compromise, especially in political or ideological contexts. It is close to obdurate but tends to be used more in the context of negotiations and disputes between groups or institutions.

"Despite the tears of his own family, the dictator remained obdurate, refusing to release the prisoners." — Here, his coldness in the face of emotional family appeals makes him obdurate.

"The committee was obdurate in its decision to close the school, brushing aside every petition and protest from the community." — Here, they are stubbornly unmoved by public pressure.

"The convicted man stood before the judge, obdurate and unrepentant, as if he saw nothing wrong with what he had done." — Here, the moral hardness and lack of remorse is the focus.

"She made every argument she could think of, but he was obdurate — his mind had been made up long before she walked into the room." — Here, the sense of an almost predetermined refusal to be persuaded comes through.
A mental image to make it stick

Picture a boulder in the middle of a river. The water — representing your arguments, your tears, your appeals to reason and conscience — flows around it, crashes against it, begs it to move. The boulder does not shift. It does not crack. It sits there, cold and hard and completely indifferent. That boulder is obdurate. Now put a human face on that boulder, and you have the word in action.
Obdurate means stubbornly hardened against change, persuasion, or remorse — unmoved by arguments, emotions, or moral pressure that would soften most people.
